All rights reserved Copyright <~ 1990 Pergamon Pt~'ss pie THE CHARACTERISTICS OF GRANULES FROM UPFLOW ANAEROBIC SLUDGE BLANKET REACTORS N. KOSAmCI, R. BLASZCZYX', L. ORPHANI and J. VALLADARESI ~The University of Western Ontario, Department of Chemical and Biochemical Engineering, London, Ontario, Canada N6A 5B9 and 2Lodz Technical University, Institute of Chemical Engineering, 90-924 Lodz, Poland (First received March 1989; accepted in revised form April 1990) Abstract--Granules from an industrial UASB reactor were maintained in bench scale (20 I.) UASB reactors and fed with a synthetic medium based on volatile fatty acids. After 60 days of reactor operation, three distinct granule types were found to have evolved within the reactors. These types were defined by their colour: black, grey and white. These granules also differed in structure (texture) and elemental composition. The proportion of black, grey and white granules in the bed changed when the organic loading rate was changed. At the low loading rate, a large number of "hollow" granules appeared which were less dense than the liquid and were washed out at the top of the reactor. Key words--anaerobic digestion, granules, loading rate, UASB reactor INTRODUCTION Granulation of methanogenic bacteria in upflow an- aerobic sludge blanket reactors (UASBR) is important in treatment of various industrial waste- waters. However, these granules occasionally dis- integrate in industrial reactors, which results in loss of activity and washout of granules from the system. Little is known about the mechanism for formation, maintenance and disintegration of granules. This paper attempts to elucidate some factors which influence granule maintenance in conditions similar to industrial reactors. Methanotrix and Methanosarcina bacteria are the main methanogens reported to form the granules. De Zeeuw and Lettinga (1980) reported that in the first stage of the granulation process (in about 10 days) filamentous bacteria, which were almost absent in the original seed sludge, grew on the external surface of a separate sludge floe, but beyond day 50 increasing numbers of Methanosarcina were observed. Little information is available on the maintenance of granules and very little on their disintegration. Tilche and Yang (1987) observed granules 0.5-3.0 rnm in diameter, the majority of them being dark, but some of them were a light grey. No significant microscopic difference was found in their bacterial composition. Dubourguier et al. (1987) showed that the granules which formed a well defined bed with a clear supernatant and without fluffy conglomerates, were black but some whitish conglomerates were always present. Bochem et al. (1982) reported that in partially cross-sectioned granules (1-3 mm in diameter) one can recognize cells consisting of two regions: a densely packed outer area and a loosely packed central area resembling a lysis zone. This latter area was comprised of ovoid cells (1.0-2.0/zm in diameter) with intercellular spaces of approx. 0.1/zm. These intercellular spaces were either completely transparent, or composed of weakly stainable matter. Beeftink and Staugard (1986) examined the colon- ization of sand grains by bacteria and found that numerical cell densities within the aggregates ranged from 1012 per ml at the periphery to very low values in the centre. Microscopic evidence for "hollowing" of large aggregates by autolysis has been presented, and it was suggested that granules lysed within large aggregates due to substrate insut~ciency (Beeftink and van den Heuvel, 1987). Conceivably, such "hollow" structures are more susceptible to shear stresses within the reactor. The disappearance of large aggregates may also have resulted from their disintegration. In this work, some features and behaviour of granules obtained from a pulp and paper mill waste- water treatment plant were investigated. It was found that during prolonged time periods, granules do change their shape, composition and density. ,MATERIALS AND METHODS Equipment Experiments were carried out in a 201. bench scale UASBR which was constructed from extruded PVC pipe having a height to diameter ratio of approx. 6 (1000 x 163 nun, respectively). Synthetic medium enters the bottom of the reactor through six equally spaced distribution ports at the circular periphery and effluent leaves by overflow from the top. The temperature was maintained at 35. A schematic of the reactor is presented in Fig. 1. w,~ ~/12--D 1473 1474 N. Kos,,~Ic et al. 1000 "-- 114 j -- R ' 163 ' "X, I,F Fig. I. Schematic of upflow anaerobic sludge blanket reactor. Effluent was recycled and combined with the influent in a ratio of about 7:1. An internal gas-liquid-solid separator cone was constructed at the top of the reactor. Pumping was provided by Piper peristaltic pumps for both the feed and recycle lines. The feed rate was 0.02251 min-t (32.51 day-I) and recycle rate 0.1641rain-t. Combined, these streams resulted in a superficial liquid upflow velocity in the reactor of 0.5 m h-t. Source of granules The granules were initially obtained from an UASBR pilot plant unit treating wastewaters from a waste paper recycling mill at Domtar Pulp and Paper Industry (Mississauga, Ontario). Medium A synthetic medium (acetic, propionic and butyric acid), modified from Trudeil et al. (1985), was used. The carbon sources were acetic acid, propionic acid and butyric acid added in a weight ratio of 4: I : I, respectively. Total COD concentration was 3800 mg I- J and COD: N: P ratio was 107:3.4:1. The pH of the medium was adjusted to 6.8 + 0.1 with 10 M NaOH. Detailed composition of the medium is given in Table I. Analysis ATP. A sample was weighed and 100/~l pipetted into a cuvette. To the samples, 100 p l of nucleotide releasing agent (NRA) was added and the cuvette placed in a LUMAC BIOCOUNTER Model 2010. An integration time of 10 s was set and 100pl of reconstituted LUMIT-PM was in- jected. After 10 s, relative light units (RLU) were read from the display and the ATP concentration was determined by means of an ATP calibration curve. ATP standard. Freeze-dried ATP (LUMAC) was recon- stituted with 10 ml of bi-distilled water and divided into 10, I ml samples. The samples were diluted to a wide range of concentrations (0.01-0.25 g ATP ml-t). From these diluted samples, I00/zl aliquots were taken and analysed as above. Volatile suspended solids (VSS). The VSS were analysed according to Standard Methods (APHA, 1975). Size of granules. Granules were distributed in a vertically placed tube by water flowing at different velocities according to the method developed by Andras et aL (1989). Washed granules were collected on filter papers and photographed. The photographic negatives were used to determine the size of granules by using a printing enlarger (Omega B22, magnification 2.2 x actual size). Calcium analysis. Atomic absorption (AA) spectroscopy (Instrumentation Laboratory Inc., Model 157) was used. The ashed sample was redissolved in 5 ml hot concentrated HCI and filtered fWhatman Qualitative No. 2) into a 50 ml volumetric flask. The 50 ml volume was made up with I ml of 10% (w/v) KCI, I ml of 5% (w/v) La203 (50 g La203 per iitre of 80% HC1 and deionized water). Scanning electron microscopy (SEM). Granules were fixed in 3% giutaraldehyde for I h, dehydrated in a graded ethanol series and critical-point dried with CO2. After sputter coating with carbon, granules were examined using an International Scientific Instruments DS-130 scanning electron microscope. Electron dispersive X-ray (EDAX) analysis. During SEM analysis the elemental composition of samples was obtained using X-ray microanalysis systems XPGT-System III. Chemical oxygen demand (COD). The COD analyses were determined by the method of Knetchel (1977). RESULTS AND DISCUSSION The reactor history The granules obtained from a UASB pilot plant exposed to pulp and paper mill wastewaters were highly contaminated with wood and fibres. Prior to reactor start-up, a known mass of granules (about 300 g of VSS) was fluidized in a liquid medium using Table i. Feed composition of synthetic medium Cone. Cone. Characteristics of granules from UASB reactors 1,175 pure nitrogen. Upon stopping the gas flow, dense granules settled first permitting removal of undesired particles along with slower settling granules. This procedure was repeated until most of the con- taminated material was flushed out. Following this procedure, the upper layer of granules was removed to leave about 240g VSS in the reactor. Upon start-up, the reactor effluent was very clear for over 1 month, and very little solids were washed out of the reactor. The initial volumetric loading rate was about 2.2 g COD 1-1 day-~, initial specific loading rate about 0.2 g COD (g VSS)-~ day-~, initial COD conversion about 80% and the initial upflow velocity 0.5 m h-~ (feed + recycle). At day 7, the volumetric load was increased to 3.8 g COD !- ~ day- ~ and about 40 g VSS were removed. At day 14 the loading rate was increased to 6.2 g COD 1-~ day-~ and maintained at this level through the experiment. The specific loading rate was about 0.65 g COD (g VSS)-t day-l. Between day 14 and day 82 accumulation of granules was observed and granules were removed at days 49 and 77 to keep the specific organic loading rate at a constant level [0.65 g COD (g VSS)-t day-t]. Increasing COD conversion values, up to 100%, were observed and larger portions of granules were removed at days 82, 118, 127 and 131 to maintain the COD conversion at 95-98%. In this way the mass of granules in the reactor decreased to about 120 g VSS and specific organic loading rate increased to about 1.0 g COD (g VSS)- 1 day- i. At day 134 another 30g VSS was removed to increase the specific organic loading rate to !.6 g COD (g VSS)- 1 day- t. Granules obserration Before start-up, all granules had a uniform dark colour. In the period of time when specific organic loading rate was about 0.65 g COD (g VSS)-t (up to day 82) the appearance of a large number of grey and white granules with diameters from 0.2 to 2 mm in the upper layer of the bed was observed. A month after start-up granules appeared in the effluent. The grey and white granules with diameters of !-2 mm predominated in the effluent although large black granules (over 2 mm in diameter) were also observed. These granules floated and sometimes did not settle even after centrifugation (at 600 g for 15 min). It is suspected that a hollow core within the granules was the reason for their poor settling. A scanning electron micrograph (SEM) of a "hollow" black granule is presented in Fig. 2. This hollow core was separated from the granular mass by a thin wall and was probably filled with gas produced by the anaerobic microbial culture within the granule. A very small mechanical stress can rupture this wall, resulting in the release of the gas within. The remaining granular mass then settles rapidly. This may suggest that an induced mechanical stress, for example by effluent recirculation could prevent the granules from maintaining this hollow core and consequently from floating out of the reactor. Fig. 2. Scanning electron micrograph of a cut "'hollow" black granule. 1476 N. Kos.~c et al. Table 2. Generally the black granules appeared to be more resistant to stresses produced by the upflow stream (0.5 m h-t) as compared to grey, which in turn were more resistant than white. The white granules col- lapsed inward, even without mechanical stress if they were partially dewatered. In comparison, the black granules kept their shape and maintained the hollow core. However, it was observed that both white and grey granules from the bottom of the reactor, settled excellently. This observation may suggest that the change of colour and the hollowing of granules resulted from different mechanisms. The "hollowing" of granules is probably connected with the size of granules. The feed may penetrate within the granules only by diffusion so when the size of the granule exceeds a certain limit, the concentration of feed in the middle of the granules becomes too small to feed the bacteria at this location resulting in starvation of the microbial population and their autolysis. It is expected that autolysis products are not so densely packed as viable cells (Bochem et al., 1982) and gas may be entrapped decreasing the density of granules, As a consequence the granules may float. A hollow core which could be visually observed may also occur. The change in colour seems to be dependent on composition of the feed around granules. Also hydro- dynamic conditions in the reactor may influence the colour of granules. When a large number of granules is packed densely at the bottom of the reactor a deficiency of some nutrients may last for a long time around granules. This may result in irreversible changes in granules composition and structure. Such a phenomenon is more possible at low specific load- ing rate and at low upflow velocities. Higher loading rates and higher upflow velocities increase the access of granules to the nutrients and may slow down the colour change of granules. It could be postulated that large grey and white granules were formed from large black granules. Due to little resistance of grey and white granules to hydraulic stresses, small grey and white granules (which were also observed) may also be formed from the disruption of large granules of these same colours. According to this hypothesis in reactors operated at low upflow velocities and low specific loading rate, the majority of granules should be grey and white and washout of large size granules should occur. In reactors operated at high upflow velocities and high specific loading rates black granules should prevail and washout of small granules should occur. Such phenomena have been observed during long term reactor performance (Kosaric et al., unpublished data). Analysis of granules Up to day 82 the loading rates were maintained at approx. 0.65 g COD (g VSS)- t day- '. The analysis of granules from the bed on this day (Table 2), in four size ranges, showed that the granular bed consisted of only a small percentage of black granules. A number of large granules, mainly grey and white, in the effluent, were also observed. Although grey and white granules predominated in the bed no change in the COD conversion and gas production was observed. The analysis of black, grey and white granules (Table 2) generally showed that the percentage of black granules is higher at higher specific loading rate. Further investigations are in progress. Granules were segregated and the ATP activity test was performed for black, grey and white granules. The results of this analysis are presented in Table 3. It was interesting to notice that the ATP activity of white granules was higher than that of the grey ones, which in turn had higher activity than the black. There is no explanation for this finding at this stage. Either the metabolic activity is indeed higher in white granules, or the ATP was merely easier to extract. EDAX analysis was performed at day 134 to find the elements present in black, grey and white granules. The granules from the bed were taken and the concentration of elements on the surface of granules was measured. The results are shown in Table 4. As one could expect, the difference in colour and physical structure between black, grey and white granules resulted from differences in surface elemental composition of the granules. The grey and white granules contained sulphur and phosphorus (about 10%), silicon and aluminium (about 4%). In contrast, black granules contained about half as much sulphur and phosphorus, and about ten times Table 3. The black colour of granules probably appears due to iron sulphides and related compounds. The elemental composition of black granules may suggest that the black colour appears when the ratio of S: Fe is small. In black granules, this ratio is about 1.8, in grey granules 5.5 and in white 8, although in white granules there is only about one-third as much iron as for the black. The high phosphorus content in grey and white granules may suggest that the sulphur is mainly combined with phosphorus. Additionally, at a high concentration of chlorine, the iron may exist as iron chloride (the ratio of CI: Fe in white granules is 0.4, but in black it is about 0.09). It is characteristic that the amount of calcium on the granule surface is almost the same in black and grey granules while just slightly lower in the white granules. This may suggest that the concentration of this element in the feed was high enough to provide Ca2+ ions to granules in excess. In fact, the calcium concentration in the feed was established at a high level of 100mgl-l, according to previous data (Mahoney et al., 1987) when calcium was shown to be beneficial for granule formation. At start-up and days 82, 134 and 160 the granules' calcium content was analysed by AA spectroscopy. At day 0 when all granules were of uniform dark colour, at day 82 when a large number of grey and white granules were observed [the specific organic loading rate of 0.65gCOD (gVSS)-Iday-~ was maintained for about 60 days], at day 134 when more dark granules were observed [the specific organic loading rate of about 1.0 g COD (g VSS)- ~ day- ' was maintained for about 50 days] and at day 160 when percentage of dark granules increased again (Table 2) and the specific organic loading rate of about 1.6 g COD (g VSS)- ~ day- ~ was maintained for 26 days. The calcium concentration in granule sludge seems to be related to the specific loading rate in the reactor (Table 5). To fully evaluate the effect of Table 5. CONCLUSIONS (I) Granules from industrial reactors, when fed with volatile fatty acids in continuous culture, can change their colour and elemental composition at varied specific organic loading rates. (2) At low specific organic loading rate [0.65 g COD (g VSS)- i day-'] granules become lighter or even white and their texture is soft. A hollow core may occur within white, grey or black granules which then may float out of the reactor. (3) At high specific organic loading rate [1.6 g COD (g VSS)-~ day-1] granules maintained their original dark coiour (mainly grey) and hollow granules rarely occurred.
